## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Convex Optimization and Applications in Machine Learning
  Official title       Convex optimization and applications in machine learning
  Instructors          A. D'ASPREMONT (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 1 · period 1 (28/09/2026 – 08/01/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 21 h (lectures 21 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Learning]{.badge .label} · domains on master-mva.com: Theory
  Language             Not displayed (the master-mva.com course page is written in French)
  Assessment           Exam (“Examen”, master-mva.com; no format or weight displayed) · Université Paris-Saclay: “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” (partial continuous assessment)
  Prerequisites        Notions of linear algebra (“Notions d’algèbre linéaire”, master-mva.com)
  Note on sources      master-mva.com announces 6 courses of 3 h; the Université Paris-Saclay table gives 21 h
  -------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with a good M1 in mathematics, computer science or physics who has already run gradient descent or called an optimization solver, and now wants to recognise convex problems, write their duals and know what the algorithms guarantee.

**Empirical first**: on a least-squares problem in dimension 500 with condition number $10^4$, a thousand steps of gradient descent bring the gap $f - f^*$ from 23.9 down to 0.012. Nesterov's accelerated method uses the same thousand gradients, plus one line of code, and reaches $3.9 \times 10^{-6}$ (code in [ch. 5](#ch5)).

An interior-point method solves a linear program with 100 constraints to eight digits in 54 Newton steps ([ch. 6](#ch6)). Why the first method is slow, why the second is optimal, and why the third barely depends on the data are the questions of this course.

The course teaches how to recognise a convex problem, how to rewrite it in one of a few standard forms (linear, quadratic, second-order cone and semidefinite programs), how to read its dual, and how the two families of algorithms that solve it work: first-order methods, which scale to huge problems, and interior-point methods, which reach high accuracy in few iterations. It ends with applications in statistics, learning, finance and signal processing, and with convex relaxations of combinatorial problems.

It shares tools with [Introduction to Statistical Learning](../s1-intro-statistical-learning/index.html) and [Foundations of Distributed and Large-Scale Computing Optimization](../s1-distributed-optimization/index.html), and prepares [Kernel Methods](../s2-kernel-methods/index.html), [Inverse Problems and Imaging](../s2-inverse-problems-imaging/index.html) and [Sequential Learning](../s2-sequential-learning/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Recognise convex sets and functions, and prove convexity with the operations that preserve it.
-   Compute projections, conjugate functions, subgradients and proximal operators of the functions used in machine learning.
-   Rewrite a modelling problem as a linear, quadratic, second-order cone or semidefinite program.
-   Derive the Lagrange dual of a convex program, check Slater's condition, and solve the KKT conditions of small problems by hand.
-   Prove the convergence rates of gradient, subgradient, proximal and accelerated methods, and explain why Nesterov's rate cannot be improved.
-   Implement Newton's method and a barrier interior-point method, and bound their number of iterations with self-concordance.
-   Formulate the LASSO, logistic regression, portfolio selection, robust constraints, total-variation denoising and sparse recovery as convex programs, and solve them.
-   Build the semidefinite relaxation of a combinatorial problem and round it, with the Goemans–Williamson guarantee for MAXCUT.
-   Read dual variables as certificates of optimality and as sensitivities of the optimal value.

### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites: notions of linear algebra. The page also uses multivariable calculus at M1 level; ch. 0 reviews everything that is needed.

-   **Refreshers** — [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) (eigenvalues, positive semidefinite matrices, gradients: the material of ch. 0), [Scientific Python](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) (NumPy and SciPy, used in every code block) and [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) (for the statistical models of ch. 8 and the randomized rounding of ch. 9).
-   **Related courses of semester 1** — [Introduction to Statistical Learning](../s1-intro-statistical-learning/index.html) studies the convex surrogate losses whose minimization is the subject here. [Foundations of Distributed and Large-Scale Computing Optimization](../s1-distributed-optimization/index.html) develops stochastic and distributed versions of the methods of ch. 5. [Optimal Transport for Machine Learning](../s1-optimal-transport-ml/index.html) starts from a linear program and its dual. [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html) and [Theoretical Foundations of Deep Learning](../s1-theoretical-foundations-dl/index.html) use the convex analysis of gradient methods as their baseline.
-   **Courses of semester 2 that build on it** — [Kernel Methods](../s2-kernel-methods/index.html) (SVM duals and quadratic programs), [Inverse Problems and Imaging](../s2-inverse-problems-imaging/index.html) (total variation, $\ell_1$ penalties, proximal algorithms), [Sequential Learning](../s2-sequential-learning/index.html) (online convex optimization), [Graphical Models: Discrete Inference and Learning](../s2-graphical-models-discrete/index.html) (linear-programming relaxations of MAP inference), [Algorithms for Network Optimization and Management](../s2-network-optimization/index.html) (linear programming and network flows) and [Reinforcement Learning](../s2-reinforcement-learning/index.html) (the linear-programming view of Markov decision processes).

### Course outline

-   **0. Review** — dual norms, the spectral theorem and Schur complements, Taylor's formula and the descent lemma, Fermat's rule.
-   **1. Convex sets** — the catalogue of convex sets, operations that preserve convexity, projection, separation and dual cones.
-   **2. Convex functions and convex analysis** — first- and second-order tests, operations, conjugates, subgradients, smoothness and strong convexity.
-   **3. Convex optimization problems** — standard form, global optimality, modelling transformations, and the hierarchy LP, QP, SOCP, SDP.
-   **4. Duality** — Lagrange duality, Slater's theorem, KKT conditions, sensitivity, conic duality.
-   **5. First-order methods and acceleration** — gradient descent, the lower complexity bound, Nesterov's method, subgradient and proximal methods.
-   **6. Newton's method and interior-point methods** — Newton's method, equality constraints, the logarithmic barrier, the central path and the barrier method.
-   **7. Self-concordance and complexity** — the affine-invariant analysis of Newton's method and the polynomial complexity of path-following methods.
-   **8. Applications** — statistics and learning, finance, signal processing: models, solvers and dual variables.
-   **9. Combinatorial problems and convex relaxations** — Lagrangian and semidefinite relaxations, MAXCUT and Goemans–Williamson rounding, convex envelopes.
-   **10. Complements for self-study** — the proof of the lower bound, the Frank–Wolfe method, primal–dual interior-point methods, mirror descent.
-   **11. Research directions and open problems** — computer-aided analysis of algorithms, restarts, fast interior-point methods, low-rank semidefinite programming, tightness of relaxations.

### How to study this module

-   Read ch. 0 before the first session if eigenvalues or Taylor's formula feel distant: every proof of ch. 2, 5 and 7 uses them.
-   After each session, redo the complete proofs without looking (Theorems 1.4, 2.2, 4.4, 4.6, 5.2, 5.5 and 7.4 are the core), then do the exercises listed in the row of the session.
-   Run the code of each chapter and change one parameter (condition number, step, $\mu$, sparsity): the printed numbers are quoted in the text, so you can check your environment.
-   The code uses only NumPy, SciPy and scikit-learn on synthetic data; every block runs in a few seconds on a laptop. Modelling tools such as CVXPY are not needed: the point is to see what they do inside.
-   Keep a one-page sheet with the conjugates of Example 2.7, the four standard forms of Definition 3.3 and the KKT conditions: the exam tests whether you can use them quickly.

## 0. Review: norms, symmetric matrices and smooth functions {#ch0}

Convex optimization uses three M1 tools constantly: norms and their duals, symmetric matrices and their eigenvalues, and Taylor expansions of smooth functions. This chapter states them in the form used later.

The [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization refresher](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) covers the same ground at a slower pace.

### Norms and dual norms

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Dual norm]{.tag} For a norm $\|\cdot\|$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the **dual norm** is
$$
\|y\|_* = \sup_{\|x\| \le 1} y^\top x .
$$
By construction $y^\top x \le \|x\| \, \|y\|_*$ for all $x, y$ (Hölder's inequality).

The Euclidean norm is its own dual. The dual of $\|\cdot\|_1$ is $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ and conversely, and the dual of $\|\cdot\|_p$ is $\|\cdot\|_q$ with $1/p + 1/q = 1$.
:::

### Symmetric matrices

::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — Spectral theorem and positive semidefinite matrices]{.tag} Every symmetric matrix $A \in \mathbb{S}^n$ writes $A = U \Lambda U^\top$ with $U$ orthogonal and $\Lambda$ real diagonal. Consequently, for all $x$,
$$
\lambda_{\min}(A) \, \|x\|_2^2 \le x^\top A x \le \lambda_{\max}(A) \, \|x\|_2^2 .
$$
$A$ is **positive semidefinite**, $A \succeq 0$, when $x^\top A x \ge 0$ for all $x$, that is when all its eigenvalues are nonnegative; $A \succ 0$ when they are positive.

The inner product on $\mathbb{S}^n$ is $\langle A, B \rangle = \mathrm{tr}(AB)$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.3 — Schur complement]{.tag} Let $C \succ 0$. Then
$$
\begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ B^\top & C \end{pmatrix} \succeq 0
\iff A - B C^{-1} B^\top \succeq 0 .
$$

::: proof
The block matrix equals $P^\top \, \mathrm{diag}(A - BC^{-1}B^\top, C) \, P$ with the invertible matrix
$$
P = \begin{pmatrix} I & 0 \\ C^{-1} B^\top & I \end{pmatrix} .
$$
A congruence by an invertible matrix preserves positive semidefiniteness, and a block-diagonal matrix is positive semidefinite exactly when its blocks are. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### Gradients, Hessians and smoothness

::: def
[Definition 0.4 — Taylor's formula with integral remainder]{.tag} For $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ twice continuously differentiable,
$$
f(y) = f(x) + \nabla f(x)^\top (y - x) + \int_0^1 (1 - s) \, (y - x)^\top \nabla^2 f(x + s(y - x)) \, (y - x) \, ds ,
$$
$$
\nabla f(y) - \nabla f(x) = \int_0^1 \nabla^2 f(x + s(y - x)) \, (y - x) \, ds .
$$
Two gradients are used throughout: $\nabla \tfrac12 \|Ax - b\|_2^2 = A^\top (Ax - b)$, and $\nabla \log\det X = X^{-1}$ on positive definite matrices.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.5 — Descent lemma]{.tag} If $\nabla f$ is $L$-Lipschitz, that is $\|\nabla f(x) - \nabla f(y)\|_2 \le L \|x - y\|_2$, then for all $x, y$
$$
f(y) \le f(x) + \nabla f(x)^\top (y - x) + \frac{L}{2} \|y - x\|_2^2 .
$$
Such an $f$ is called **$L$-smooth**.

::: proof
By the fundamental theorem of calculus along the segment,
$$
f(y) - f(x) - \nabla f(x)^\top (y - x) = \int_0^1 \big(\nabla f(x + s(y - x)) - \nabla f(x)\big)^\top (y - x) \, ds .
$$
By Cauchy–Schwarz and the Lipschitz bound, the integrand is at most $L s \|y - x\|_2^2$, whose integral is $\frac{L}{2}\|y - x\|_2^2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### Optimality without inequality constraints

::: prop
[Proposition 0.6 — Fermat's rule and Lagrange multipliers]{.tag} If $x^*$ is a local minimum of a differentiable $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, then $\nabla f(x^*) = 0$, and $\nabla^2 f(x^*) \succeq 0$ if $f$ is twice differentiable.

Now add the constraint $h(x) = 0$, with $h : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^p$ continuously differentiable.

If $x^*$ is a local minimum of $f$ under this constraint, and the Jacobian of $h$ at $x^*$ has rank $p$, there exists $\nu \in \mathbb{R}^p$ with
$$
\nabla f(x^*) + \sum_{j=1}^p \nu_j \nabla h_j(x^*) = 0 .
$$
These conditions are only necessary. For convex problems they become sufficient (ch. 2 and 4), which is the first reason convexity matters.
:::

::: ex
[Example 0.7 — A badly conditioned quadratic]{.tag} Let $f(x) = \frac12 (x_1^2 + 100 x_2^2)$. Its gradient is $(x_1, 100 x_2)$ and its Hessian is $\mathrm{diag}(1, 100)$.

So $f$ is $L$-smooth with $L = 100$, and the minimizer is $0$.

The gradient step $x - \nabla f(x)/L$ maps $(x_1, x_2)$ to
$$
(0.99 \, x_1, \ 0) .
$$
The steep coordinate is solved in one step, but the flat one shrinks by only 1 % per step: about 460 steps to divide it by 100. The ratio 100 of the extreme curvatures, the condition number, sets the speed of gradient methods (ch. 5).
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   The dual norm turns $y^\top x$ into a product of norms; $\ell_1$ and $\ell_\infty$ are dual, $\ell_2$ is self-dual.
-   Positive semidefiniteness is read on eigenvalues, and block matrices are tested by Schur complements.
-   Taylor's formula with integral remainder gives the descent lemma: an $L$-smooth function lies below a quadratic.
-   Stationarity is necessary for a minimum; convexity will make it sufficient.
:::

## 1. Convex sets {#ch1}

Every convex program optimizes over a convex set, and every duality argument rests on separating convex sets by hyperplanes. This chapter lists the convex sets used in the course, the operations that preserve convexity, and the two geometric tools: projection and separation.

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Convex set, cone, convex hull]{.tag} A set $C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is **convex** if $\theta x + (1 - \theta) y \in C$ for all $x, y \in C$ and $\theta \in [0, 1]$.

It is a **cone** if $\theta x \in C$ for all $x \in C$ and $\theta \ge 0$, and a **convex cone** if it is both.

The **convex hull** $\mathrm{conv}\, S$ is the set of convex combinations $\sum_i \theta_i x_i$ of points of $S$, with $\theta_i \ge 0$ and $\sum_i \theta_i = 1$. It is the smallest convex set containing $S$.
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.2 — The catalogue]{.tag}

-   **Hyperplanes** $\{x : a^\top x = b\}$ and **halfspaces** $\{x : a^\top x \le b\}$, with $a \neq 0$.
-   **Norm balls** $\{x : \|x - x_c\| \le r\}$ and **ellipsoids** $\{x_c + P u : \|u\|_2 \le 1\}$.
-   **Polyhedra** $\{x : Ax \preceq b, \ Cx = d\}$, where $\preceq$ is componentwise; the probability simplex is one.
-   The **second-order cone** $\{(u, t) : \|u\|_2 \le t\}$.
-   The **positive semidefinite cone** $\mathbb{S}^n_+$. It is convex because it is the intersection, over all $z$, of the halfspaces $\{X : z^\top X z \ge 0\}$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.3 — Operations that preserve convexity]{.tag}

-   Intersection of any family of convex sets.
-   Image and inverse image under an affine map $x \mapsto Ax + b$.
-   Image and inverse image under the perspective map $(z, t) \mapsto z/t$ on $t > 0$, and under linear-fractional maps.

For example, the solution set of a **linear matrix inequality**, $\{x : x_1 A_1 + \dots + x_n A_n \preceq B\}$ with symmetric $A_i$ and $B$, is convex. It is the inverse image of the cone $\mathbb{S}^m_+$ under the affine map $x \mapsto B - \sum_i x_i A_i$.

::: proof
For affine images: if $y_1 = Ax_1 + b$ and $y_2 = Ax_2 + b$ with $x_1, x_2 \in C$, then
$$
\theta y_1 + (1 - \theta) y_2 = A\big(\theta x_1 + (1 - \theta) x_2\big) + b
$$
is the image of a point of $C$. Inverse images and intersections are checked the same way; for perspectives, see Boyd and Vandenberghe (2004, §2.3). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### Projection and separation

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.4 — Projection onto a closed convex set]{.tag} Let $C$ be nonempty, closed and convex, and $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$. There is a unique point $P_C(x) \in C$ closest to $x$ in Euclidean norm. It is characterised by
$$
\big(x - P_C(x)\big)^\top \big(z - P_C(x)\big) \le 0 \quad \text{for all } z \in C .
$$
Moreover $P_C$ is non-expansive:
$$
\|P_C(x) - P_C(y)\|_2 \le \|x - y\|_2 .
$$

::: proof
-   *Existence*: for any $z_0 \in C$, minimize the continuous function $z \mapsto \|x - z\|_2$ on the compact set of points of $C$ at distance at most $\|x - z_0\|_2$ from $x$.
-   *Characterization*: let $p = P_C(x)$, $z \in C$ and $\theta \in (0, 1]$. The point $p + \theta (z - p)$ is in $C$, so expanding $\|x - p - \theta(z - p)\|_2^2 \ge \|x - p\|_2^2$ gives
$$
-2\theta \, (x - p)^\top (z - p) + \theta^2 \|z - p\|_2^2 \ge 0 .
$$
Divide by $\theta$ and let $\theta \to 0$. Conversely, if the inequality holds, then for every $z \in C$
$$
\|x - z\|^2 = \|x - p\|^2 - 2(x - p)^\top (z - p) + \|z - p\|^2 \ge \|x - p\|^2 .
$$
-   *Uniqueness and non-expansiveness*: with $p = P_C(x)$ and $q = P_C(y)$, add the characterizations $(x - p)^\top (q - p) \le 0$ and $(y - q)^\top (p - q) \le 0$. This gives
$$
\|p - q\|_2^2 \le (x - y)^\top (p - q) \le \|x - y\|_2 \, \|p - q\|_2 .
$$
With $x = y$ it forces $p = q$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.5 — Separating and supporting hyperplanes]{.tag}

1.  If $C$ is nonempty, closed and convex and $x_0 \notin C$, there are $a \neq 0$ and $b$ with $a^\top z \le b < a^\top x_0$ for all $z \in C$ (strict separation).
2.  If $C$ and $D$ are disjoint nonempty convex sets, there are $a \ne 0$ and $b$ such that
    $$
    a^\top x \le b \ \text{ on } C, \qquad a^\top x \ge b \ \text{ on } D .
    $$
3.  At every boundary point $x_0$ of a convex set $C$ there is a **supporting hyperplane**: some $a \neq 0$ with $a^\top z \le a^\top x_0$ for all $z \in C$.

Consequently, a closed convex set is the intersection of the halfspaces that contain it.

::: proof
Part 1: let $p = P_C(x_0)$ and $a = x_0 - p \neq 0$. Theorem 1.4 gives $a^\top z \le a^\top p$ for all $z \in C$, and $a^\top x_0 - a^\top p = \|a\|_2^2 > 0$. Take $b = a^\top p$.

Part 3: take points $x_k$ outside the closure of $C$ converging to $x_0$, separate them by Part 1 with unit normals $a_k$, and extract a convergent subsequence of the $a_k$.

Part 2: apply the same limiting argument to the convex set $C - D$, which does not contain $0$ (Boyd and Vandenberghe 2004, §2.5). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 1.6 — Dual cone and generalized inequality]{.tag} The **dual cone** of a cone $K$ is
$$
K^* = \{ y : y^\top x \ge 0 \text{ for all } x \in K \} .
$$
A closed convex cone $K$ with nonempty interior that contains no line is called **proper**. It defines the **generalized inequality** $x \preceq_K y \iff y - x \in K$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.7 — Self-dual cones]{.tag} The nonnegative orthant, the second-order cone and $\mathbb{S}^n_+$ are **self-dual**: $K^* = K$. The dual of the norm cone $\{(x, t) : \|x\| \le t\}$ is the cone $\{(y, s) : \|y\|_* \le s\}$ of the dual norm.

::: proof
For $\mathbb{S}^n_+$: if $X, Y \succeq 0$, then $\mathrm{tr}(XY) = \mathrm{tr}(X^{1/2} Y X^{1/2}) \ge 0$, so $\mathbb{S}^n_+ \subseteq (\mathbb{S}^n_+)^*$.

Conversely, if $\mathrm{tr}(XY) \ge 0$ for all $X \succeq 0$, take $X = z z^\top$: then $z^\top Y z \ge 0$ for all $z$, so $Y \succeq 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 1.8 — Projection onto the simplex]{.tag} The projection onto the probability simplex $\Delta = \{x \succeq 0, \ \mathbf{1}^\top x = 1\}$ has the form
$$
P_\Delta(v) = \max(v - \tau \mathbf{1}, \ 0) ,
$$
where the threshold $\tau$ makes the result sum to 1. Sorting $v$ finds $\tau$ in $O(n \log n)$ operations.

The code checks the characterization of Theorem 1.4 on 10 000 random points of the simplex: the largest value of $(v - P_\Delta(v))^\top (z - P_\Delta(v))$ is $-6.2 \times 10^{-4}$, negative as it must be.
:::

```python
import numpy as np

def proj_simplex(v):
    """Euclidean projection of v onto {x >= 0, sum(x) = 1} (sort-based)."""
    u = np.sort(v)[::-1]
    css = np.cumsum(u) - 1.0
    k = np.arange(1, v.size + 1)
    rho = np.nonzero(u - css / k > 0)[0][-1]   # last index with a positive entry
    tau = css[rho] / (rho + 1)
    return np.maximum(v - tau, 0.0)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
v = rng.normal(size=6)
p = proj_simplex(v)
print("v      =", np.round(v, 3))
print("P(v)   =", np.round(p, 3), " sum =", p.sum().round(12))

# Check the obtuse-angle characterization (Theorem 1.4) on random simplex points
Z = rng.dirichlet(np.ones(6), size=10_000)
print("max_z (v - P(v))^T (z - P(v)) =", ((Z - p) @ (v - p)).max().round(12))
```

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   Halfspaces, balls, ellipsoids, polyhedra, the second-order cone and the semidefinite cone are the building blocks; intersections and affine maps preserve convexity.
-   The projection onto a closed convex set exists, is unique, is characterised by an obtuse-angle inequality, and is non-expansive.
-   Separation and supporting hyperplanes follow from the projection; they are the engine of duality in ch. 4.
-   The orthant, the second-order cone and the semidefinite cone are self-dual, which is why their duals look like the primals.
:::

## 2. Convex functions and convex analysis {#ch2}

Convex functions are the objectives and constraints of convex programs. This chapter gives the tests that recognise them, the operations that build new ones, and the three objects of convex analysis that every algorithm uses: the conjugate, the subdifferential, and the smoothness and strong-convexity constants.

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Convex, strictly convex and strongly convex functions]{.tag} A function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$ with convex domain $\mathrm{dom}\, f = \{x : f(x) < \infty\}$ is **convex** if, for $x, y \in \mathrm{dom}\, f$ and $\theta \in [0, 1]$,
$$
f(\theta x + (1 - \theta) y) \le \theta f(x) + (1 - \theta) f(y) .
$$
Equivalently, its **epigraph** $\{(x, t) : f(x) \le t\}$ is a convex set.

It is **strictly convex** if the inequality is strict for $x \neq y$ and $\theta \in (0, 1)$, and **$\mu$-strongly convex** ($\mu > 0$) if $f - \frac{\mu}{2}\|\cdot\|_2^2$ is convex. It is **concave** if $-f$ is convex.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.2 — First- and second-order conditions]{.tag} Let $f$ be differentiable on an open convex domain. Then $f$ is convex if and only if
$$
f(y) \ge f(x) + \nabla f(x)^\top (y - x) \quad \text{for all } x, y .
$$
If $f$ is twice differentiable, $f$ is convex if and only if $\nabla^2 f(x) \succeq 0$ for all $x$.

The tangent plane is a global under-estimator: local information gives a global bound. In particular, $\nabla f(x^*) = 0$ makes $x^*$ a global minimizer.

::: proof
-   ($\Rightarrow$) For $\theta \in (0, 1]$, convexity gives $f(x + \theta(y - x)) \le f(x) + \theta (f(y) - f(x))$. Subtract $f(x)$, divide by $\theta$ and let $\theta \to 0$.
-   ($\Leftarrow$) Let $z = \theta x + (1 - \theta) y$. Write the inequality at $z$ towards both points, multiply by $\theta$ and $1 - \theta$, and add. The gradient terms cancel, leaving
    $$
    \theta f(x) + (1 - \theta) f(y) \ge f(z) .
    $$
-   Second order: if $\nabla^2 f \succeq 0$, the remainder in Taylor's formula (Definition 0.4) is nonnegative, which is the first-order condition.
-   Conversely, $g(s) = f(x + s v)$ is convex. Adding the first-order inequality at $s$ towards 0 and at 0 towards $s$ gives $(g'(s) - g'(0)) s \ge 0$. So $g'$ is nondecreasing, and
    $$
    g''(0) = v^\top \nabla^2 f(x) v \ge 0 .
    $$
    [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 2.3 — A catalogue of convex functions]{.tag}

-   On $\mathbb{R}$: the exponential $e^{ax}$, the negative logarithm $-\log x$ and the negative entropy $x \log x$.
-   The powers $x^p$ on $x > 0$, for $p \ge 1$ or $p \le 0$.
-   Every norm, by the triangle inequality and homogeneity.
-   $\max_i x_i$, and its smooth version **log-sum-exp** $f(x) = \log \sum_i e^{x_i}$, which satisfies
$$
\max_i x_i \le f(x) \le \max_i x_i + \log n .
$$
-   The **quadratic-over-linear** function $x^2 / y$ on $y > 0$, and $-\log\det X$ on positive definite matrices.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.4 — Two Hessian computations]{.tag} Log-sum-exp is convex, and $\log\det$ is concave on positive definite matrices.

::: proof
-   With $z_i = e^{x_i}$, the Hessian of log-sum-exp is
$$
\nabla^2 f(x) = \frac{\mathrm{diag}(z)}{\mathbf{1}^\top z} - \frac{z z^\top}{(\mathbf{1}^\top z)^2} ,
$$
and $v^\top \nabla^2 f(x) v \ge 0$ is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $(\sum_i z_i v_i)^2 \le (\sum_i z_i)(\sum_i z_i v_i^2)$.
-   For $\log\det$, restrict to a line $X = Z + tV$ with $Z \succ 0$. With $\lambda_i$ the eigenvalues of $Z^{-1/2} V Z^{-1/2}$,
$$
\log\det(Z + tV) = \log\det Z + \sum_i \log(1 + t \lambda_i) ,
$$
a sum of concave functions of $t$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.5 — Operations that preserve convexity]{.tag}

-   Nonnegative weighted sums, and composition with an affine map, $x \mapsto f(Ax + b)$.
-   Pointwise supremum $f(x) = \sup_{y \in \mathcal{A}} g(x, y)$ of functions convex in $x$: its epigraph is an intersection of epigraphs. Example: $\lambda_{\max}(X) = \sup_{\|y\|_2 = 1} y^\top X y$ is convex.
-   Composition $h(g(x))$ with $h$ convex and nondecreasing and $g$ convex (and the other sign rules of the composition calculus).
-   Partial minimization $g(x) = \inf_{y \in C} f(x, y)$ of a jointly convex $f$ over a convex set $C$, when $g > -\infty$. Example: the distance to a convex set.
-   Perspective $(x, t) \mapsto t f(x / t)$ on $t > 0$.

Jensen's inequality $f(\mathbb{E} X) \le \mathbb{E} f(X)$ extends Definition 2.1 to all probability distributions.

::: proof
For partial minimization: given $x_1, x_2$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, pick $y_i \in C$ with $f(x_i, y_i) \le g(x_i) + \varepsilon$. Joint convexity gives
$$
g(\theta x_1 + (1 - \theta) x_2) \le f\big(\theta x_1 + (1 - \theta) x_2, \ \theta y_1 + (1 - \theta) y_2\big) \le \theta g(x_1) + (1 - \theta) g(x_2) + \varepsilon .
$$
Let $\varepsilon \to 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### Conjugate functions

::: def
[Definition 2.6 — Convex conjugate]{.tag} The **conjugate** of $f$ is
$$
f^*(y) = \sup_{x \in \mathrm{dom} f} \big( y^\top x - f(x) \big) .
$$
It is convex, as a supremum of affine functions of $y$, even when $f$ is not. It satisfies the **Fenchel–Young inequality** $f(x) + f^*(y) \ge x^\top y$.

If $f$ is convex and closed (lower semicontinuous), then $f^{**} = f$: this is the Fenchel–Moreau theorem (Rockafellar 1970, §12).
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.7 — Conjugates used later]{.tag}

| $f(x)$ | $f^*(y)$ |
|---|---|
| $\frac12 x^\top Q x$, $Q \succ 0$ | $\frac12 y^\top Q^{-1} y$ |
| $\|x\|$ (any norm) | $0$ if $\|y\|_* \le 1$, $+\infty$ otherwise |
| $-\log x$ on $x > 0$ | $-1 - \log(-y)$ on $y < 0$ |
| $\sum_i x_i \log x_i$ on the simplex | $\log \sum_i e^{y_i}$ |
| $e^x$ | $y \log y - y$ on $y \ge 0$ (value 0 at $y = 0$) |

For the norm, suppose first $\|y\|_* > 1$. Some $x$ with $\|x\| \le 1$ has $y^\top x > 1$, and its multiples $tx$ make $t(y^\top x - \|x\|)$ unbounded.

If instead $\|y\|_* \le 1$, then $y^\top x \le \|x\|$ for all $x$, with equality at $x = 0$, so the supremum is 0.
:::

### Subgradients

::: def
[Definition 2.8 — Subgradient and subdifferential]{.tag} A vector $g$ is a **subgradient** of a convex $f$ at $x$ if
$$
f(y) \ge f(x) + g^\top (y - x) \quad \text{for all } y .
$$
The set $\partial f(x)$ of subgradients is the **subdifferential**. It is closed and convex, it equals $\{\nabla f(x)\}$ where $f$ is differentiable, and it is nonempty at every interior point of the domain: apply the supporting hyperplane theorem (Theorem 1.5) to the epigraph at $(x, f(x))$.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 2.9 — Fermat's rule and subdifferential calculus]{.tag}

-   $x^*$ minimizes a convex $f$ if and only if $0 \in \partial f(x^*)$, by the definition.
-   The subdifferential of a sum contains the sum of the subdifferentials, with equality when the relative interiors of the domains intersect (Rockafellar 1970, §23):
    $$
    \partial (f_1 + f_2)(x) \supseteq \partial f_1(x) + \partial f_2(x) .
    $$
-   $\partial |x| = \{\mathrm{sign}(x)\}$ for $x \neq 0$ and $[-1, 1]$ at 0; $\partial \|x\|_1$ is the product of these sets.
-   For any norm, $\partial \|x\| = \{ g : \|g\|_* \le 1, \ g^\top x = \|x\| \}$.
-   For $f = \max_i f_i$ with differentiable convex $f_i$, $\partial f(x)$ is the convex hull of the gradients of the $f_i$ that attain the maximum.
:::

### Smoothness and strong convexity

::: prop
[Proposition 2.10 — Two-sided quadratic bounds]{.tag} If $f$ is $L$-smooth (Proposition 0.5) and $\mu$-strongly convex, then for all $x, y$
$$
\frac{\mu}{2} \|y - x\|_2^2 \le f(y) - f(x) - \nabla f(x)^\top (y - x) \le \frac{L}{2} \|y - x\|_2^2 .
$$
For twice differentiable $f$ this reads $\mu I \preceq \nabla^2 f \preceq L I$. The ratio $\kappa = L / \mu$ is the **condition number**.

Minimizing both bounds over $y$ gives, with $f^* = \min f$,
$$
\frac{1}{2L} \|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2 \le f(x) - f^* \le \frac{1}{2\mu} \|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2 .
$$
The left inequality needs only smoothness; it says that a large gradient means a large gap.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   Convexity is tested by the tangent inequality or by a positive semidefinite Hessian; restricting to lines reduces matrix functions to one variable.
-   Sums, affine compositions, suprema, partial minimization and perspectives preserve convexity: this calculus is how convexity is proved in practice.
-   The conjugate is always convex; its table turns into a table of duals in ch. 4.
-   Subgradients extend gradients to nonsmooth functions, and $0 \in \partial f(x^*)$ characterizes minimizers.
-   The constants $L$ and $\mu$ sandwich $f$ between two quadratics; their ratio $\kappa$ governs first-order methods.
:::

## 3. Convex optimization problems {#ch3}

A convex program minimizes a convex function over a set described by convex inequalities and affine equalities. This chapter gives the standard form, the property that makes these problems tractable (every local minimum is global), and the hierarchy of conic programs into which modelling translates applied problems.

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Convex program in standard form]{.tag}
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{minimize} & f_0(x) \\
\text{subject to} & f_i(x) \le 0, \quad i = 1, \dots, m, \\
& Ax = b ,
\end{array}
$$
with $f_0, \dots, f_m$ convex. The **optimal value** $p^*$ is the infimum of $f_0$ over the feasible set: $+\infty$ if it is empty, $-\infty$ if $f_0$ is unbounded below on it.

A feasible $x$ is **$\varepsilon$-suboptimal** if $f_0(x) \le p^* + \varepsilon$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.2 — Local minima are global; optimality condition]{.tag} For a convex program, every locally optimal point is globally optimal, and the optimal set is convex. If $f_0$ is differentiable, a feasible $x$ is optimal if and only if
$$
\nabla f_0(x)^\top (y - x) \ge 0 \quad \text{for every feasible } y .
$$

::: proof
-   Let $x$ be locally optimal and suppose a feasible $y$ has $f_0(y) < f_0(x)$. The points $x + \theta (y - x)$ are feasible, and by convexity, for every $\theta \in (0, 1]$,
    $$
    f_0\big(x + \theta (y - x)\big) \le (1 - \theta) f_0(x) + \theta f_0(y) < f_0(x) .
    $$
    Arbitrarily small $\theta$ gives points arbitrarily close to $x$ with a smaller value, which contradicts local optimality.
-   The optimal set is the intersection of the feasible set with the sublevel set $\{f_0 \le p^*\}$, two convex sets.
-   Sufficiency of the condition is Theorem 2.2: $f_0(y) \ge f_0(x) + \nabla f_0(x)^\top (y - x) \ge f_0(x)$.
-   Necessity: if $\nabla f_0(x)^\top (y - x) < 0$ for a feasible $y$, small steps from $x$ towards $y$ stay feasible and decrease $f_0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### Equivalent problems

Modelling means rewriting a problem until a standard form appears. Four transformations are used constantly.

-   **Epigraph form**: minimize $t$ subject to $f_0(x) \le t$ and the constraints, which makes the objective linear.
-   **Slack variables**: an affine inequality $a^\top x \le b$ becomes $a^\top x + s = b$ with $s \ge 0$.
-   **Splitting**: $x = x^+ - x^-$ with $x^\pm \succeq 0$ linearizes absolute values.
-   **New variables**: $\min_x \sum_i |a_i^\top x - b_i|$ becomes the linear program
$$
\text{minimize } \mathbf{1}^\top t \quad \text{s.t.} \quad -t \preceq Ax - b \preceq t .
$$

### The conic hierarchy

::: def
[Definition 3.3 — LP, QP, SOCP, SDP]{.tag}

-   **Linear program (LP)**: minimize $c^\top x$ subject to $Gx \preceq h$ and $Ax = b$.
-   **Quadratic program (QP)**: minimize $\frac12 x^\top P x + q^\top x$ with $P \succeq 0$, under affine constraints. A QCQP also allows convex quadratic constraints.
-   **Second-order cone program (SOCP)**: minimize $f^\top x$ subject to $Fx = g$ and
$$
\|A_i x + b_i\|_2 \le c_i^\top x + d_i , \quad i = 1, \dots, m .
$$
-   **Semidefinite program (SDP)**: minimize $c^\top x$ subject to $Ax = b$ and the linear matrix inequality
$$
x_1 F_1 + \dots + x_n F_n + G \preceq 0 , \qquad F_i, G \in \mathbb{S}^k .
$$
Its standard form is: minimize $\mathrm{tr}(CX)$ subject to $\mathrm{tr}(A_i X) = b_i$ and $X \succeq 0$.

Each class contains the previous one: LP $\subset$ QP $\subset$ QCQP $\subset$ SOCP $\subset$ SDP.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.4 — From quadratic to cone to semidefinite constraints]{.tag}

-   A convex quadratic constraint $x^\top P x + s(x) \le 0$, with $P = R^\top R$ and $s(x) = q^\top x + r$ affine, is the second-order cone constraint
$$
\left\| \begin{pmatrix} 2 R x \\ 1 + s(x) \end{pmatrix} \right\|_2 \le 1 - s(x) .
$$
-   A second-order cone constraint is a linear matrix inequality:
$$
\|u\|_2 \le t \iff \begin{pmatrix} t I & u \\ u^\top & t \end{pmatrix} \succeq 0 .
$$

::: proof
-   If the cone constraint holds, its right-hand side $1 - s$ is nonnegative, and squaring gives $4\|Rx\|_2^2 + (1 + s)^2 \le (1 - s)^2$, that is $\|Rx\|_2^2 \le -s$. Conversely, $\|Rx\|_2^2 \le -s$ gives $s \le 0$, so $1 - s > 0$ and the square root of the squared inequality is the cone constraint.
-   For $t > 0$, the Schur complement (Proposition 0.3) with respect to the scalar block $t$ gives $tI - u u^\top / t \succeq 0$, that is $t^2 \ge \|u\|_2^2$.
-   For $t = 0$, both sides force $u = 0$: a positive semidefinite matrix with a zero diagonal entry has a zero row. For $t < 0$ both sides fail. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 3.5 — Modelling with the hierarchy]{.tag}

-   $\ell_\infty$ regression $\min \|Ax - b\|_\infty$ is the LP: minimize $t$ subject to $-t \mathbf{1} \preceq Ax - b \preceq t \mathbf{1}$.
-   Least squares with bounds on $x$ is a QP.
-   A **robust** constraint $a^\top x \le b$ for every $a$ in the ellipsoid $\{\bar a + P u : \|u\|_2 \le 1\}$ is an SOC constraint. Indeed $\sup_{\|u\|_2 \le 1} (Pu)^\top x = \|P^\top x\|_2$, so it reads
$$
\bar a^\top x + \|P^\top x\|_2 \le b .
$$
-   Minimizing the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\max}(A_0 + \sum_i x_i A_i)$ is the SDP: minimize $t$ subject to $A_0 + \sum_i x_i A_i \preceq t I$.
:::

::: ex
[Example 3.6 — The Chebyshev centre of a polyhedron is an LP]{.tag} The ball $\{x_c + u : \|u\|_2 \le r\}$ lies in the halfspace $a_i^\top x \le b_i$ if and only if $a_i^\top x_c + r \|a_i\|_2 \le b_i$, because the supremum of $a_i^\top u$ over the ball is $r \|a_i\|_2$ (Definition 0.1). Maximizing $r$ under these linear constraints is an LP.

For the triangle $x \succeq 0$, $x_1 + x_2 \le 4$, cut by $x_1 - 2 x_2 \le 2$, the code finds the incircle of the triangle:
$$
x_c = (1.1716, \ 1.1716), \qquad r = 4 - 2\sqrt{2} = 1.1716 .
$$
The fourth constraint is inactive (slack 0.55) and the solver reports a zero dual variable for it, a fact that complementary slackness will explain.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import linprog

# Polyhedron {x : a_i^T x <= b_i}: a triangle cut by a fourth half-plane
A = np.array([[-1.0, 0.0], [0.0, -1.0], [1.0, 1.0], [1.0, -2.0]])
b = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 4.0, 2.0])

# Chebyshev centre: maximize r s.t. a_i^T x + r ||a_i||_2 <= b_i  (variables x1, x2, r)
norms = np.linalg.norm(A, axis=1)
res = linprog(c=[0, 0, -1], A_ub=np.c_[A, norms], b_ub=b,
              bounds=[(None, None), (None, None), (0, None)], method="highs")
xc, r = res.x[:2], res.x[2]
print("centre =", np.round(xc, 4), " radius =", round(r, 4))
print("slacks b - A xc - r||a|| =", np.round(b - A @ xc - r * norms, 4))
print("dual variables (marginals) =", np.round(-res.ineqlin.marginals, 4))
```

::: note
[Modelling languages]{.tag} CVX (Grant and Boyd 2008) and CVXPY (Diamond and Boyd 2016) implement the rules of Proposition 2.5: an expression is accepted when its convexity follows from the composition rules. It is then rewritten, with the transformations above, into a conic program handed to an interior-point or first-order solver. The code on this page uses only NumPy and SciPy, to show what such tools do inside.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   In a convex program every local minimum is global, and optimality is a first-order condition on feasible directions.
-   Epigraphs, slacks, splitting and auxiliary variables turn applied problems into standard forms.
-   LP, QP, SOCP and SDP form a nested hierarchy; Schur complements move constraints up the hierarchy.
-   Robust and norm constraints are second-order cone constraints; eigenvalue constraints are semidefinite.
:::

## 4. Duality {#ch4}

Every optimization problem comes with a dual: a concave maximization whose value bounds the primal optimum from below. When the bound is tight, the dual variables certify optimality, measure the sensitivity of the optimum to the constraints, and often give a simpler problem to solve.

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Lagrangian and dual function]{.tag} For the problem of Definition 3.1, convex or not, the **Lagrangian** is
$$
L(x, \lambda, \nu) = f_0(x) + \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i f_i(x) + \nu^\top (Ax - b) ,
$$
and the **dual function** is $g(\lambda, \nu) = \inf_x L(x, \lambda, \nu)$, the infimum being over the common domain $\mathcal{D}$ of the $f_i$. As a pointwise infimum of affine functions of $(\lambda, \nu)$, $g$ is concave.

The **dual problem** maximizes $g(\lambda, \nu)$ over $\lambda \succeq 0$; its value is $d^*$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Weak duality]{.tag} For every $\lambda \succeq 0$ and every $\nu$, $g(\lambda, \nu) \le p^*$. Hence
$$
d^* \le p^* .
$$

::: proof
For feasible $x$, each $\lambda_i f_i(x) \le 0$ and $Ax - b = 0$, so $g(\lambda, \nu) \le L(x, \lambda, \nu) \le f_0(x)$. Take the infimum over feasible $x$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

For a feasible $x$ and a dual feasible $(\lambda, \nu)$, the **duality gap** $f_0(x) - g(\lambda, \nu)$ bounds the suboptimality of $x$. It is the stopping criterion of the solvers of ch. 6.
::::

::: ex
[Example 4.3 — Three duals]{.tag}

-   **LP** in standard form: minimize $c^\top x$ subject to $Ax = b$, $x \succeq 0$. The Lagrangian $c^\top x - \lambda^\top x + \nu^\top (Ax - b)$ is affine in $x$.

    It is bounded below only if $c + A^\top \nu - \lambda = 0$. With $y = -\nu$, the dual is
$$
\text{maximize } b^\top y \quad \text{s.t.} \quad A^\top y \preceq c .
$$
-   **Least norm**: minimize $\|x\|_2^2$ subject to $Ax = b$. The Lagrangian is minimized at $x = -A^\top \nu / 2$, and
$$
g(\nu) = -\tfrac14 \nu^\top A A^\top \nu - b^\top \nu .
$$
-   **Through conjugates**: for minimize $f_0(x)$ subject to $Ax \preceq b$ and $Cx = d$,
$$
g(\lambda, \nu) = -b^\top \lambda - d^\top \nu - f_0^*(-A^\top \lambda - C^\top \nu) ,
$$
so the table of conjugates (Example 2.7) is a table of duals.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.4 — Slater's theorem]{.tag} Suppose the problem is convex and satisfies **Slater's condition**: some $\tilde x$ in the relative interior of $\mathcal{D}$ is strictly feasible, $f_i(\tilde x) < 0$ for all $i$ and $A \tilde x = b$. Then strong duality holds, and the dual optimum is attained when $p^*$ is finite:
$$
d^* = p^* .
$$
Affine inequalities need not hold strictly; in particular a feasible LP with finite value has a zero duality gap.

::: proof
We prove it with inequality constraints only and $p^*$ finite; equality constraints add a relative-interior argument (Boyd and Vandenberghe 2004, §5.3.2).

-   Consider the set of pairs $(u, t)$ achievable by some point of the domain:
    $$
    \mathcal{A} = \{ (u, t) : \exists x \in \mathcal{D}, \ f_i(x) \le u_i \text{ for all } i, \ f_0(x) \le t \} .
    $$
    It is convex because the $f_i$ are. It does not meet $\mathcal{B} = \{(0, s) : s < p^*\}$.
-   Theorem 1.5 gives $(\tilde\lambda, \mu) \ne 0$ and $\alpha$ with $\tilde\lambda^\top u + \mu t \ge \alpha$ on $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mu t \le \alpha$ on $\mathcal{B}$.
-   $\mathcal{A}$ is unbounded upwards in every coordinate, so $\tilde\lambda \succeq 0$ and $\mu \ge 0$. Letting $s \to p^*$ in $\mathcal{B}$ gives $\mu p^* \le \alpha$.
-   If $\mu > 0$, take $(u, t) = (f(x), f_0(x))$ and divide by $\mu$. This gives, for all $x \in \mathcal{D}$,
    $$
    L(x, \tilde\lambda / \mu) \ge p^* .
    $$
    So $g(\tilde\lambda / \mu) \ge p^*$, and weak duality makes $\tilde\lambda / \mu$ dual optimal with $d^* = p^*$.
-   If $\mu = 0$, then $\tilde\lambda \neq 0$, $\alpha \ge 0$, and $\sum_i \tilde\lambda_i f_i(x) \ge 0$ for all $x \in \mathcal{D}$. At the Slater point the left-hand side is negative: a contradiction. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 4.5 — When Slater's condition fails]{.tag} Minimize $e^{-x}$ subject to $x^2 / y \le 0$, on the domain $y > 0$. The constraint forces $x = 0$, so $p^* = 1$.

The dual function is $g(\lambda) = \inf_{x, \, y > 0} (e^{-x} + \lambda x^2 / y) = 0$: take $x$ large and $y$ much larger. So $d^* = 0$, a duality gap of 1. No point is strictly feasible.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.6 — Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions]{.tag} Let $f_0, \dots, f_m$ be differentiable. The **KKT conditions** at $(x, \lambda, \nu)$ are:

-   primal feasibility: $f_i(x) \le 0$ for all $i$, and $Ax = b$;
-   dual feasibility: $\lambda \succeq 0$;
-   complementary slackness: $\lambda_i f_i(x) = 0$ for all $i$;
-   stationarity:
    $$
    \nabla f_0(x) + \sum_i \lambda_i \nabla f_i(x) + A^\top \nu = 0 .
    $$

For a convex problem, every KKT point is primal and dual optimal, with zero gap. Under Slater's condition, conversely, $x$ is optimal if and only if some $(\lambda, \nu)$ satisfies the KKT conditions with it.

::: proof
-   Sufficiency: $L(\cdot, \lambda, \nu)$ is convex since $\lambda \succeq 0$, and stationary at $x$, so $x$ minimizes it (Theorem 2.2). By complementary slackness and feasibility, $g(\lambda, \nu) = L(x, \lambda, \nu) = f_0(x)$, and weak duality makes both optimal.
-   Necessity: let $x^*$ be optimal and $(\lambda^*, \nu^*)$ dual optimal (Theorem 4.4). Then
$$
f_0(x^*) = g(\lambda^*, \nu^*) \le L(x^*, \lambda^*, \nu^*) \le f_0(x^*) .
$$
Both inequalities are equalities. The second gives $\sum_i \lambda_i^* f_i(x^*) = 0$, a sum of nonpositive terms, hence complementary slackness. The first says that $x^*$ minimizes $L(\cdot, \lambda^*, \nu^*)$, hence stationarity. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.7 — Sensitivity and shadow prices]{.tag} Perturb the constraints to $f_i(x) \le u_i$ and $Ax - b = v$, and let $p^*(u, v)$ be the optimal value. If strong duality holds with dual optimum $(\lambda^*, \nu^*)$, then for all $(u, v)$
$$
p^*(u, v) \ge p^*(0, 0) - \lambda^{*\top} u - \nu^{*\top} v .
$$
Where $p^*$ is differentiable, $\partial p^* / \partial u_i = -\lambda_i^*$. A large multiplier marks a constraint whose tightening is expensive; in economics, $\lambda_i^*$ is the price of resource $i$.

::: proof
Let $x$ be feasible for the perturbed problem. Then $\lambda_i^* f_i(x) \le \lambda_i^* u_i$ and $Ax - b = v$, so
$$
p^*(0, 0) = g(\lambda^*, \nu^*) \le L(x, \lambda^*, \nu^*) \le f_0(x) + \lambda^{*\top} u + \nu^{*\top} v .
$$
Take the infimum over such $x$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 4.8 — Semidefinite duality]{.tag} The dual of the SDP
$$
\text{minimize } c^\top x \quad \text{s.t.} \quad x_1 F_1 + \dots + x_n F_n + G \preceq 0
$$
is the SDP
$$
\text{maximize } \mathrm{tr}(G Z) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \mathrm{tr}(F_i Z) + c_i = 0, \ i = 1, \dots, n, \qquad Z \succeq 0 .
$$
The multiplier of a matrix inequality is a positive semidefinite matrix, because $\mathbb{S}^k_+$ is self-dual (Proposition 1.7). As in Theorem 4.4, strong duality holds when the primal is strictly feasible.
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.9 — Water-filling]{.tag} To allocate a unit of power to $n$ channels with noise levels $\alpha_i > 0$ and maximize capacity, solve
$$
\text{minimize } -\sum_{i=1}^n \log(\alpha_i + x_i) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad x \succeq 0, \ \mathbf{1}^\top x = 1 .
$$
The KKT conditions are $x_i \ge 0$, $\lambda_i \ge 0$, $\lambda_i x_i = 0$ and $-1/(\alpha_i + x_i) - \lambda_i + \nu = 0$. Eliminating $\lambda$ gives
$$
x_i = \max\Big(0, \ \frac{1}{\nu} - \alpha_i\Big) ,
$$
where the **water level** $1/\nu$ is fixed by $\mathbf{1}^\top x = 1$: the channels are filled up to a common level.

For $\alpha = (0.2, 0.5, 0.9, 1.6)$, bisection finds the level $1/\nu = 0.85$, and
$$
x^* = (0.65, \ 0.35, \ 0, \ 0), \qquad \lambda^* = (0, \ 0, \ 0.065, \ 0.551) .
$$
The two noisiest channels receive nothing, and their multipliers are positive.
:::

```python
import numpy as np

alpha = np.array([0.2, 0.5, 0.9, 1.6])          # noise levels of 4 channels
def x_of(nu):                                   # KKT solution for a given multiplier
    return np.maximum(0.0, 1.0 / nu - alpha)

lo, hi = 1e-6, 1e6                              # bisection on the "water level" 1/nu
for _ in range(200):
    nu = np.sqrt(lo * hi)
    lo, hi = (nu, hi) if x_of(nu).sum() > 1.0 else (lo, nu)
x = x_of(nu)
lam = nu - 1.0 / (alpha + x)                    # multipliers of x >= 0
print("water level 1/nu =", round(1 / nu, 4))
print("x* =", np.round(x, 4), " sum =", round(x.sum(), 6))
print("lambda* =", np.round(lam, 4) + 0.0)        # + 0.0 turns -0.0 into 0.0
print("complementary slackness max |lambda_i x_i| =", np.abs(lam * x).max().round(10))
print("optimal value =", round(-np.log(alpha + x).sum(), 4))
```

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 4

-   The dual function is concave and bounds the primal value from below, convex or not (weak duality).
-   Under Slater's condition the bound is tight; the proof is one separating hyperplane.
-   The KKT conditions characterize optimality of convex problems under Slater's condition; complementary slackness says which constraints matter.
-   Dual variables are sensitivities of the optimal value, and the multiplier of a matrix inequality is a positive semidefinite matrix.
:::

## 5. First-order methods and acceleration {#ch5}

When the dimension is large, a Newton step costs too much and one uses gradients only. This chapter proves how fast gradient methods converge, shows that no gradient method can beat a rate of order $1/k^2$ on smooth convex functions, and gives Nesterov's method, which attains it. Proximal versions extend everything to nonsmooth regularizers.

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — First-order method]{.tag} A first-order method queries an oracle that returns $f(x)$ and $\nabla f(x)$, or a subgradient, and produces iterates with
$$
x_k \in x_0 + \mathrm{span}\{\nabla f(x_0), \dots, \nabla f(x_{k-1})\} .
$$
Its **complexity** on a class of functions is the number of oracle calls needed to guarantee $f(x_k) - f^* \le \varepsilon$ (Nemirovski and Yudin 1983).
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.2 — Gradient descent]{.tag} Let $f$ be convex and $L$-smooth with a minimizer $x^*$, and $x_{k+1} = x_k - \frac1L \nabla f(x_k)$. Then
$$
f(x_k) - f^* \le \frac{L \|x_0 - x^*\|_2^2}{2k} .
$$
If $f$ is also $\mu$-strongly convex,
$$
\|x_k - x^*\|_2^2 \le \Big(1 - \frac{\mu}{L}\Big)^k \|x_0 - x^*\|_2^2 .
$$

::: proof
Write $g = \nabla f(x_k)$.

-   The descent lemma (Proposition 0.5) gives $f(x_{k+1}) \le f(x_k) - \frac{1}{2L}\|g\|^2$: the values decrease.
-   Convexity gives $f(x_k) \le f^* + g^\top (x_k - x^*)$. Adding, and expanding $\|x_{k+1} - x^*\|^2 = \|x_k - x^* - g/L\|^2$,
$$
f(x_{k+1}) - f^* \le g^\top (x_k - x^*) - \frac{1}{2L}\|g\|^2 = \frac{L}{2}\big(\|x_k - x^*\|^2 - \|x_{k+1} - x^*\|^2\big) .
$$
-   Summing from $0$ to $k - 1$ telescopes: the sum of the $k$ gaps $f(x_1) - f^*, \dots, f(x_k) - f^*$ is at most $\frac{L}{2}\|x_0 - x^*\|^2$. The gaps decrease, so the last one is at most their average.
-   Strongly convex case: Proposition 2.10, with $y = x^*$, gives
    $$
    g^\top (x_k - x^*) \ge f(x_k) - f^* + \frac{\mu}{2}\|x_k - x^*\|^2 ,
    $$
    and the first step, with $f^* \le f(x_{k+1})$, gives $\|g\|^2 / L^2 \le 2 (f(x_k) - f^*) / L$. Insert both in
$$
\|x_{k+1} - x^*\|^2 = \|x_k - x^*\|^2 - \frac{2}{L} g^\top (x_k - x^*) + \frac{1}{L^2}\|g\|^2 .
$$
The function gaps cancel and $\|x_{k+1} - x^*\|^2 \le (1 - \mu / L)\|x_k - x^*\|^2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: thm
[Theorem 5.3 — Lower complexity bound]{.tag} For every $k$ with $1 \le k \le (n - 1)/2$ and every $x_0$, there is a convex $L$-smooth quadratic $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ such that every first-order method satisfies
$$
f(x_k) - f^* \ge \frac{3 L \|x_0 - x^*\|_2^2}{32 (k + 1)^2} .
$$
The worst function (Nesterov 2004, §2.1) is
$$
f(x) = \frac{L}{4}\Big(\frac12 x^\top A x - x_1\Big) ,
$$
where $A$ is tridiagonal with 2 on the diagonal and $-1$ beside it, on the first $2k + 1$ coordinates.

From $x_0 = 0$, each gradient reveals one more coordinate, so $x_k$ lives on the first $k$ coordinates, far from the minimizer. The complete computation is in ch. 10.
:::

### Nesterov's accelerated gradient method

::: def
[Algorithm 5.4 — Accelerated gradient method (Nesterov 1983)]{.tag} Start from $z_0 = x_0$ and set $\theta_k = 2/(k + 2)$. For $k = 0, 1, \dots$
$$
y_k = (1 - \theta_k) x_k + \theta_k z_k, \qquad x_{k+1} = y_k - \tfrac{1}{L}\nabla f(y_k), \qquad z_{k+1} = z_k - \tfrac{1}{\theta_k L}\nabla f(y_k) .
$$
Eliminating $z$ gives the familiar momentum form:
$$
x_{k+1} = y_k - \tfrac{1}{L}\nabla f(y_k), \qquad y_{k+1} = x_{k+1} + \frac{k}{k + 3}(x_{k+1} - x_k) .
$$
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.5 — The accelerated rate]{.tag} For convex $L$-smooth $f$, Algorithm 5.4 satisfies, for $k \ge 1$:

::: key
[Key result — Nesterov's rate]{.tag}
$$
f(x_k) - f^* \le \frac{2 L \|x_0 - x^*\|_2^2}{(k + 1)^2}
$$
:::

By Theorem 5.3 no first-order method can do better than this rate, up to a factor $64/3 \approx 21$.

::: proof
Let $g = \nabla f(y_k)$ and $r_k = \|z_k - x^*\|^2$.

-   Descent lemma: $f(x_{k+1}) \le f(y_k) - \frac{1}{2L}\|g\|^2$.
-   Convexity at $y_k$, towards $x_k$ with weight $1 - \theta_k$ and towards $x^*$ with weight $\theta_k$:
$$
f(y_k) \le (1 - \theta_k) f(x_k) + \theta_k f^* + g^\top \big(y_k - (1 - \theta_k) x_k - \theta_k x^*\big) ,
$$
and $y_k - (1 - \theta_k) x_k = \theta_k z_k$, so the last term is $\theta_k g^\top (z_k - x^*)$.
-   Expanding the square in the $z$-update gives
    $$
    \theta_k g^\top (z_k - x^*) = \frac{\theta_k^2 L}{2}(r_k - r_{k+1}) + \frac{1}{2L}\|g\|^2 .
    $$
-   The three lines combine into
$$
f(x_{k+1}) - f^* \le (1 - \theta_k)\big(f(x_k) - f^*\big) + \frac{\theta_k^2 L}{2}(r_k - r_{k+1}) .
$$
-   Divide by $\theta_k^2$ and note that
    $$
    \frac{1 - \theta_k}{\theta_k^2} = \frac{k(k + 2)}{4} \le \frac{(k + 1)^2}{4} = \frac{1}{\theta_{k-1}^2} .
    $$
    The quantity $\theta_{k-1}^{-2}(f(x_k) - f^*) + \frac{L}{2} r_k$ never increases, and at $k = 0$ the coefficient $(1 - \theta_0)/\theta_0^2$ is zero.
-   Hence $\theta_k^{-2}(f(x_{k+1}) - f^*) \le \frac{L}{2} r_0$, which is the claim since $\theta_k = 2/(k + 2)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Strong convexity]{.tag} When $\mu > 0$ is known, the constant momentum $(\sqrt{\kappa} - 1)/(\sqrt{\kappa} + 1)$ contracts the error by $1 - 1/\sqrt{\kappa}$ per step instead of $1 - 1/\kappa$ (Nesterov 2004, §2.2). For $\kappa = 10^4$ this needs about 100 times fewer iterations.

Restarting Algorithm 5.4 every $\lceil\sqrt{8\kappa}\rceil$ steps recovers this rate up to a constant factor, but the period needs $\kappa$. Adaptive restarts, which need no knowledge of $\mu$, do as well in practice (Ex. 15).
:::

::: ex
[Example 5.6 — Acceleration on a badly conditioned quadratic]{.tag} The code minimizes a quadratic in dimension 500 with eigenvalues from $10^{-4}$ to 1, so $\kappa = 10^4$, from $f(x_0) = 23.9$.

| iterations $K$ | 10 | 100 | 1000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| gradient descent | 1.14 | 0.133 | 0.0116 |
| accelerated | 0.573 | 0.0076 | $3.9 \times 10^{-6}$ |

Both stay below their bounds (Theorems 5.2 and 5.5). Acceleration gains a factor 3000 at $K = 1000$ for the cost of one extra line.
:::

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 500
Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(n, n)))
eig = np.logspace(-4, 0, n)                     # mu = 1e-4, L = 1: condition number 1e4
H = (Q * eig) @ Q.T
xstar = rng.normal(size=n)
f = lambda x: 0.5 * (x - xstar) @ H @ (x - xstar)  # f* = 0
grad = lambda x: H @ (x - xstar)
L, x0 = eig.max(), np.zeros(n)

def gd(K):
    x = x0.copy()
    for _ in range(K):
        x = x - grad(x) / L
    return f(x)

def agd(K):                                     # Nesterov, momentum k/(k+3)
    x_prev = x = y = x0.copy()
    for k in range(K):
        x_prev, x = x, y - grad(y) / L
        y = x + k / (k + 3) * (x - x_prev)
    return f(x)

R2 = np.sum((x0 - xstar) ** 2)
print(f"f(x0) = {f(x0):.3f}")
for K in (10, 100, 1000):
    print(f"K={K:5d}  GD {gd(K):.2e}  AGD {agd(K):.2e}  "
          f"bound L R^2/(2K) {L * R2 / (2 * K):.2e}  bound 2LR^2/(K+1)^2 {2 * L * R2 / (K + 1)**2:.2e}")
```

### Nonsmooth functions: the subgradient method

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.7 — Subgradient method]{.tag} Let $f$ be convex and $G$-Lipschitz, so that every subgradient has $\|g\|_2 \le G$, and let $\|x_0 - x^*\|_2 \le R$. The iteration $x_{i+1} = x_i - \alpha_i g_i$ with $g_i \in \partial f(x_i)$ satisfies
$$
\min_{i \le k} f(x_i) - f^* \le \frac{R^2 + G^2 \sum_{i=0}^k \alpha_i^2}{2 \sum_{i=0}^k \alpha_i} .
$$
The constant step $\alpha_i = R / (G \sqrt{k + 1})$ gives
$$
\min_{i \le k} f(x_i) - f^* \le \frac{R G}{\sqrt{k + 1}} .
$$

::: proof
Expand the square:
$$
\|x_{i+1} - x^*\|^2 = \|x_i - x^*\|^2 - 2\alpha_i g_i^\top (x_i - x^*) + \alpha_i^2 \|g_i\|^2 ,
$$
and use $g_i^\top (x_i - x^*) \ge f(x_i) - f^*$ (Definition 2.8). Summing over $i = 0, \dots, k$ gives
$$
2 \sum_{i=0}^k \alpha_i \big(f(x_i) - f^*\big) \le R^2 + G^2 \sum_{i=0}^k \alpha_i^2 .
$$
Bound each $f(x_i)$ below by the minimum. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The rate $1/\sqrt{k}$ is optimal for nonsmooth Lipschitz functions (Nemirovski and Yudin 1983): nonsmoothness, not the dimension, makes these problems slow.
::::

### Proximal gradient methods

::: def
[Definition 5.8 — Proximal operator]{.tag} For a closed convex $h$ and $\gamma > 0$,
$$
\mathrm{prox}_{\gamma h}(v) = \arg\min_x \Big( h(x) + \frac{1}{2\gamma}\|x - v\|_2^2 \Big) ,
$$
well defined because the objective is strongly convex. The indicator of a closed convex set gives the projection onto it. For $h = \|\cdot\|_1$, Fermat's rule (Proposition 2.9) gives **soft thresholding**:
$$
\mathrm{prox}_{\gamma \|\cdot\|_1}(v)_i = \mathrm{sign}(v_i) \max(|v_i| - \gamma, 0) .
$$
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 5.9 — ISTA and FISTA]{.tag} Let $F = f + h$ with $f$ convex and $L$-smooth and $h$ closed convex. The **proximal gradient** iteration
$$
x_{k+1} = \mathrm{prox}_{h/L}\big(x_k - \tfrac{1}{L}\nabla f(x_k)\big)
$$
satisfies $F(x_k) - F^* \le L\|x_0 - x^*\|^2 / (2k)$. Its accelerated version FISTA (Beck and Teboulle 2009) satisfies $F(x_k) - F^* \le 2L\|x_0 - x^*\|^2 / (k + 1)^2$. With $h = \lambda \|\cdot\|_1$, the first is called ISTA.

The proofs of Theorems 5.2 and 5.5 use smoothness and convexity only through one inequality, which still holds for $F$. For $x^+$ the proximal step from $y$ and $G = L(y - x^+)$, for every $z$:
$$
F(z) \ge F(x^+) + G^\top (z - y) + \frac{1}{2L}\|G\|_2^2 .
$$
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 5

-   Gradient descent with step $1/L$ converges as $1/k$ on smooth convex functions, and linearly at rate $1 - 1/\kappa$ under strong convexity.
-   No first-order method beats $1/k^2$ on smooth convex functions; Nesterov's method attains it with one extra momentum step.
-   On nonsmooth Lipschitz functions the subgradient method converges as $1/\sqrt{k}$, which is optimal.
-   Proximal steps handle nonsmooth regularizers at the price of a projection-like operation: ISTA and FISTA keep the rates of the smooth case.
:::

## 6. Newton's method and interior-point methods {#ch6}

Interior-point methods solve linear, second-order cone and semidefinite programs to high accuracy in a few dozen Newton steps. This chapter builds them in three moves: Newton's method for smooth problems, its extension to equality constraints, and the logarithmic barrier that turns inequality constraints into a smooth penalty.

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Newton step and Newton decrement]{.tag} For $f$ twice differentiable with $\nabla^2 f(x) \succ 0$,
$$
\Delta x_{\mathrm{nt}} = -\nabla^2 f(x)^{-1} \nabla f(x), \qquad \lambda(x) = \big(\nabla f(x)^\top \nabla^2 f(x)^{-1} \nabla f(x)\big)^{1/2} .
$$
The step minimizes the second-order Taylor model of $f$ at $x$, and $\lambda(x)^2 / 2$ is the decrease the model predicts.

Both are **affine invariant**: minimizing $y \mapsto f(Ty)$, for an invertible $T$, instead of $f$ maps the iterates by $T$ and leaves $\lambda$ unchanged.
:::

::: def
[Algorithm 6.2 — Damped Newton method with backtracking]{.tag} Given $x \in \mathrm{dom}\, f$, a tolerance $\varepsilon$, $\alpha \in (0, 1/2)$ and $\beta \in (0, 1)$, repeat:

1.  compute $\Delta x_{\mathrm{nt}}$ and $\lambda(x)$; stop if $\lambda(x)^2 / 2 \le \varepsilon$;
2.  line search: start from $s = 1$ and multiply $s$ by $\beta$ as long as
    $$
    f(x + s \Delta x_{\mathrm{nt}}) > f(x) - \alpha s \lambda(x)^2 ;
    $$
3.  update $x \leftarrow x + s \Delta x_{\mathrm{nt}}$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.3 — Local quadratic convergence]{.tag} Suppose $\nabla^2 f \succeq m I$ near the minimizer $x^*$, and $\nabla^2 f$ is $M$-Lipschitz there. Then the full Newton step $x_{k+1} = x_k + \Delta x_{\mathrm{nt}}$ satisfies
$$
\|x_{k+1} - x^*\|_2 \le \frac{M}{2m} \|x_k - x^*\|_2^2 .
$$
Once $\frac{M}{2m}\|x_k - x^*\|_2 < 1$, the error is squared at each step: the number of correct digits doubles.

::: proof
Since $\nabla f(x^*) = 0$, the integral form of Definition 0.4 gives, with $H_k = \nabla^2 f(x_k)$,
$$
x_{k+1} - x^* = H_k^{-1} \int_0^1 \big( H_k - \nabla^2 f(x^* + s(x_k - x^*)) \big) (x_k - x^*) \, ds .
$$
The integrand has norm at most $M (1 - s) \|x_k - x^*\|^2$, so the integral is at most $\frac{M}{2}\|x_k - x^*\|^2$, and $\|H_k^{-1}\| \le 1/m$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 6.4 — Newton step with equality constraints]{.tag} To minimize $f(x)$ subject to $Ax = b$ from a feasible $x$, the Newton step minimizes the quadratic model over the directions with $A \Delta x = 0$. By the KKT conditions (Theorem 4.6) it solves
$$
\begin{pmatrix} \nabla^2 f(x) & A^\top \\ A & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \Delta x_{\mathrm{nt}} \\ w \end{pmatrix} =
\begin{pmatrix} -\nabla f(x) \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} ,
$$
where $w$ estimates the multiplier $\nu$. The iterates stay feasible, and the analysis is unchanged.
:::

### The logarithmic barrier and the central path

::: def
[Definition 6.5 — Logarithmic barrier and central path]{.tag} For the convex program of Definition 3.1, with twice differentiable $f_i$ and a strictly feasible point, the **logarithmic barrier** is
$$
\phi(x) = -\sum_{i=1}^m \log(-f_i(x)) ,
$$
convex and infinite on the boundary of the feasible set. For $t > 0$, the **central point** $x^*(t)$ minimizes $t f_0(x) + \phi(x)$ subject to $Ax = b$.

The curve $t \mapsto x^*(t)$ is the **central path**: as $t$ grows, the barrier weighs less and $x^*(t)$ moves towards a solution.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.6 — Central points are $m/t$-suboptimal]{.tag} Every central point gives a dual feasible pair, $\lambda_i^*(t) = -1/(t f_i(x^*(t)))$ and $\nu^*(t) = w / t$, where $w$ is the multiplier of the centering problem. Consequently
$$
f_0(x^*(t)) - p^* \le \frac{m}{t} .
$$

::: proof
The optimality condition of the centering problem at $x^* = x^*(t)$ reads
$$
t \nabla f_0(x^*) + \sum_i \frac{1}{-f_i(x^*)} \nabla f_i(x^*) + A^\top w = 0 .
$$
Divided by $t$, it says that $x^*$ minimizes $L(\cdot, \lambda^*(t), \nu^*(t))$, with $\lambda^*(t) \succ 0$.

Moreover $Ax^* = b$, and $\lambda_i^*(t) f_i(x^*) = -1/t$ for each $i$. Hence
$$
g(\lambda^*(t), \nu^*(t)) = f_0(x^*) + \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i^*(t) f_i(x^*) = f_0(x^*) - \frac{m}{t} ,
$$
and weak duality concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The centrality conditions are the KKT conditions with complementary slackness relaxed to $-\lambda_i f_i(x) = 1/t$.
::::

::: def
[Algorithm 6.7 — Barrier method]{.tag} Given a strictly feasible $x$, $t = t^{(0)} > 0$, $\mu > 1$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, repeat:

1.  **centering**: compute $x^*(t)$ by Newton's method (Algorithm 6.2 with Proposition 6.4), starting from the current $x$;
2.  update $x \leftarrow x^*(t)$;
3.  stop if $m/t \le \varepsilon$; otherwise set $t \leftarrow \mu t$.

Besides the initial centering, at $t^{(0)}$, the method performs one centering per update of $t$, and the number of updates is
$$
\Big\lceil \frac{\log\big(m / (\varepsilon t^{(0)})\big)}{\log \mu} \Big\rceil .
$$
A strictly feasible start comes from a **phase I** problem: minimize $s$ subject to $f_i(x) \le s$ and $Ax = b$. It starts from any $x$ with $Ax = b$ and a large $s$.
:::

::: ex
[Example 6.8 — A barrier method for a linear program]{.tag} The code minimizes $c^\top x$ subject to 100 random inequalities $a_i^\top x \le b_i$ in dimension 50, with the barrier $-\sum_i \log(b_i - a_i^\top x)$, $\mu = 20$ and $\varepsilon = 10^{-7}$.

The formula above predicts 1 + 7 = 8 centerings. Each takes between 5 and 9 Newton steps while the gap $m/t$ falls from 100 to $7.8 \times 10^{-8}$: 54 Newton steps in total. The value agrees with the HiGHS solver to $4 \times 10^{-8}$.

A larger $\mu$ means fewer centerings but more Newton steps per centering; Ex. 6 measures the trade-off.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import linprog

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
m, n = 100, 50
A = rng.normal(size=(m, n))
b = rng.uniform(1, 2, size=m)                   # x = 0 is strictly feasible
c = -A.T @ rng.uniform(0, 1, size=m)            # c = -A^T lambda, lambda >= 0: LP is bounded

def centering(x, t, tol=1e-9, max_steps=50):
    """Newton's method with backtracking on t c^T x - sum log(b - A x)."""
    F = lambda z: t * c @ z - np.log(b - A @ z).sum()
    for steps in range(max_steps):
        d = 1.0 / (b - A @ x)
        g = t * c + A.T @ d
        Hs = A.T @ (A * d[:, None] ** 2)
        dx = -np.linalg.solve(Hs, g)
        lam2 = -g @ dx                          # Newton decrement squared
        if lam2 / 2 <= tol:
            break
        s = 1.0
        while np.min(b - A @ (x + s * dx)) <= 0:
            s *= 0.5                            # stay inside the domain
        while F(x + s * dx) > F(x) - 0.25 * s * lam2 and s > 1e-8:
            s *= 0.5                            # Armijo backtracking, alpha = 0.25
        x = x + s * dx
    return x, steps

x, t, mu, eps, total = np.zeros(n), 1.0, 20.0, 1e-7, 0
while True:                                     # Algorithm 6.7
    x, k = centering(x, t)
    total += k
    print(f"t = {t:9.1e}  Newton steps = {k:2d}  duality gap m/t = {m / t:.1e}")
    if m / t <= eps:                            # stopping rule of step 3
        break
    t *= mu
ref = linprog(c, A_ub=A, b_ub=b, bounds=[(None, None)] * n, method="highs")
print(f"barrier: {c @ x:.8f}   HiGHS: {ref.fun:.8f}   total Newton steps: {total}")
```

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 6

-   Newton's method is affine invariant and converges quadratically near a minimizer; the Newton decrement measures the distance to it.
-   Equality constraints add a KKT linear system and change nothing else.
-   The logarithmic barrier replaces inequalities by a smooth penalty; its minimizers form the central path.
-   Each central point carries a dual certificate with gap exactly $m/t$, so the barrier method knows when to stop.
:::

## 7. Self-concordance and complexity {#ch7}

The classical analysis of Newton's method depends on constants $m$ and $M$ that change with the coordinates, although the method itself does not. Nesterov and Nemirovski (1994) found the affine-invariant condition that makes the analysis exact, self-concordance, and with it a polynomial bound on the number of Newton steps of interior-point methods.

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Self-concordant function]{.tag} A convex function $f$ of one variable, three times differentiable on an open interval, is **self-concordant** if
$$
|f'''(x)| \le 2 f''(x)^{3/2} .
$$
A convex $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is self-concordant if every restriction $t \mapsto f(x + tv)$ to a line is. The **local norm** at $x$ is $\|h\|_x = (h^\top \nabla^2 f(x) h)^{1/2}$, and $\lambda(x) = \|\Delta x_{\mathrm{nt}}\|_x$.
:::

::: ex
[Example 7.2 — Self-concordant functions]{.tag}

-   $-\log x$: here $f'' = 1/x^2$ and $f''' = -2/x^3$, with equality in the definition. Affine and convex quadratic functions have $f''' = 0$.
-   The class is closed under sums, affine changes of variable, and multiplication by a constant $a \ge 1$.
-   Hence the LP barrier $-\sum_i \log(b_i - a_i^\top x)$ is self-concordant, and so are $-\log\det X$ and $-\log(t^2 - \|u\|_2^2)$ on the second-order cone (Nesterov and Nemirovski 1994).
-   $e^x$ is not self-concordant on $\mathbb{R}$ (Ex. 11).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.3 — Hessian control along a segment]{.tag} Let $f$ be self-concordant and $r = \|y - x\|_x < 1$. Then for $s \in [0, 1]$
$$
(y - x)^\top \nabla^2 f(x + s(y - x)) (y - x) \le \frac{r^2}{(1 - s r)^2} ,
$$
and, with $\omega_*(r) = -r - \log(1 - r)$,
$$
f(y) \le f(x) + \nabla f(x)^\top (y - x) + \omega_*(r) .
$$

::: proof
-   Let $\varphi(s) = f(x + s(y - x))$. Self-concordance says that the derivative of $\varphi''(s)^{-1/2}$, which is $-\frac12 \varphi''' \varphi''^{-3/2}$, has absolute value at most 1.
-   Since $\varphi''(0) = r^2$, integrating this bound gives
    $$
    \varphi''(s)^{-1/2} \ge \varphi''(0)^{-1/2} - s = \frac{1 - sr}{r} ,
    $$
    which is the first inequality.
-   Insert it in Taylor's formula (Definition 0.4); a direct computation gives $\int_0^1 (1 - s) \frac{r^2}{(1 - sr)^2} ds = \omega_*(r)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The **Dikin ellipsoid** $\{y : \|y - x\|_x < 1\}$ lies in the domain of $f$ when $f$ tends to infinity at the boundary of its domain (Nesterov 2004, §4.1).
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 7.4 — Newton's method on self-concordant functions]{.tag} Let $f$ be self-concordant, bounded below, and tend to infinity at the boundary of its domain. Let $\omega(t) = t - \log(1 + t)$.

1.  The damped step $x^+ = x + \frac{1}{1 + \lambda(x)} \Delta x_{\mathrm{nt}}$ stays in the domain and decreases $f$ by at least $\omega(\lambda(x))$.
2.  If $\lambda(x) < 1$, the full step satisfies
$$
\lambda(x^+) \le \Big( \frac{\lambda(x)}{1 - \lambda(x)} \Big)^2 .
$$
3.  Damped steps while $\lambda \ge 1/4$, then full steps, reach $f(x) - f^* \le \varepsilon$ after at most
$$
\frac{f(x_0) - f^*}{\omega(1/4)} + \log_2 \log_2 \frac{1}{\varepsilon} + c
$$
Newton steps, for an absolute constant $c$; here $\omega(1/4) \approx 0.0269$. No constant of $f$ appears.

::: proof
Part 1: the step has local norm $r = \lambda / (1 + \lambda) < 1$, and $\nabla f(x)^\top (x^+ - x) = -\lambda^2 / (1 + \lambda)$. Proposition 7.3 gives
$$
f(x^+) \le f(x) - \frac{\lambda^2}{1 + \lambda} - \frac{\lambda}{1 + \lambda} + \log(1 + \lambda) = f(x) - \omega(\lambda) .
$$
Part 2 uses the matrix form of Proposition 7.3 (Nesterov 2004, §4.1).

Part 3: while $\lambda \ge 1/4$, each step gains at least $\omega(1/4)$. Afterwards Part 2 gives $\lambda^+ \le \frac{16}{9}\lambda^2$, and $f(x) - f^* \le \omega_*(\lambda) \le \lambda^2$ for $\lambda \le 0.68$ (Nesterov 2004, §4.1). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 7.5 — The two phases, observed]{.tag} The code computes the analytic centre of 200 random halfspaces in $\mathbb{R}^{20}$, starting close to several faces. Twelve damped steps bring $\lambda$ from 4.7 to 0.23. Three full steps then give
$$
\lambda = 3.8 \times 10^{-3}, \quad 2.2 \times 10^{-6}, \quad 1.2 \times 10^{-12} ,
$$
the doubling of digits of Theorem 7.4. The worst-case bound of Part 3 allows 833 damped steps; twelve were needed.
:::

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
m, n = 200, 20
A = rng.normal(size=(m, n))
b = rng.uniform(0.01, 1.0, size=m)              # x = 0 is strictly feasible, close to some faces
f = lambda x: -np.log(b - A @ x).sum()          # self-concordant (sum of -log of affine)

x, k = np.zeros(n), 0
while True:
    d = 1.0 / (b - A @ x)
    g, H = A.T @ d, A.T @ (A * d[:, None] ** 2)
    dx = -np.linalg.solve(H, g)
    lam = np.sqrt(-g @ dx)                      # Newton decrement lambda(x)
    print(f"k = {k:2d}  f = {f(x):10.6f}  lambda = {lam:.2e}")
    if lam < 1e-10:
        break
    step = 1.0 if lam < 0.25 else 1.0 / (1.0 + lam)   # damped phase, then pure Newton
    x, k = x + step * dx, k + 1
print("bound on damped steps: (f(x0) - f*) / omega(1/4) =",
      round((f(np.zeros(n)) - f(x)) / (0.25 - np.log(1.25)), 1))
```

### Self-concordant barriers and the complexity of path following

::: def
[Definition 7.6 — Self-concordant barrier]{.tag} A self-concordant $\varphi$ whose domain is the interior of a closed convex set $K$ is a **$\vartheta$-self-concordant barrier** for $K$ if
$$
\nabla \varphi(x)^\top \nabla^2 \varphi(x)^{-1} \nabla \varphi(x) \le \vartheta \quad \text{for all } x .
$$
Three examples are used throughout:

-   $-\sum_{i=1}^m \log(b_i - a_i^\top x)$ for a polyhedron with $m$ faces, with $\vartheta = m$;
-   $-\log\det X$ for $\mathbb{S}^n_+$, with $\vartheta = n$;
-   $-\log(t^2 - \|u\|_2^2)$ for the second-order cone, with $\vartheta = 2$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 7.7 — Complexity of path following]{.tag} Minimize a linear objective by Algorithm 6.7 with exact centering, with the logarithmic barrier of $m = \vartheta$ inequalities. The barriers of the second-order and semidefinite cones, with the parameters of Definition 7.6, behave the same way (Boyd and Vandenberghe 2004, §11.6). When $t$ becomes $\mu t$, the new centering problem starts at most
$$
\vartheta \, (\mu - 1 - \log \mu)
$$
above its minimum, so it costs at most $\vartheta(\mu - 1 - \log\mu)/\omega(1/4) + c'$ Newton steps (Theorem 7.4).

With $\mu = 1 + 1/\sqrt{\vartheta}$, this is a constant number of Newton steps per centering, since $\mu - 1 - \log \mu \le (\mu - 1)^2 / 2$. The total number of Newton steps is then
$$
O\Big( \sqrt{\vartheta} \, \log \frac{\vartheta}{t^{(0)} \varepsilon} \Big) .
$$

::: proof
For the logarithmic barrier with $m = \vartheta$ inequalities, let $x = x^*(t)$, $x^+ = x^*(\mu t)$ and $(\lambda, \nu)$ the dual pair of Proposition 6.6, so that $-f_i(x) = 1/(t \lambda_i)$. The gap of the new centering problem equals
$$
\mu t f_0(x) - \mu t f_0(x^+) + \sum_i \log\big(-\mu t \lambda_i f_i(x^+)\big) - m \log \mu .
$$
-   By $\log a \le a - 1$, the sum is at most $-\mu t \sum_i \lambda_i f_i(x^+) - m$.
-   Since $Ax^+ = b$, the definition of the dual function gives
    $$
    f_0(x^+) + \sum_i \lambda_i f_i(x^+) = L(x^+, \lambda, \nu) \ge g(\lambda, \nu) .
    $$
-   By Proposition 6.6, $f_0(x) - g(\lambda, \nu) = m/t$. Together, the gap is at most $\mu m - m - m\log\mu$.

For general $\vartheta$-self-concordant barriers, the same $O(\sqrt{\vartheta}\log(1/\varepsilon))$ bound holds with a different analysis; see Nesterov and Nemirovski (1994) and Renegar (2001). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Primal–dual methods]{.tag} Practical solvers use primal–dual variants that update $x$, $\lambda$ and $\nu$ together, by Newton steps on the relaxed KKT system, with Mehrotra's predictor–corrector (Mehrotra 1992). They need a few tens of iterations on most problems, almost independently of the size; each iteration solves one linear system, which is the real cost. Ch. 10 sketches them.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 7

-   Self-concordance, $|f'''| \le 2 f''^{3/2}$, is affine invariant; logarithms of affine, log-determinant and second-order cone barriers satisfy it.
-   On self-concordant functions, damped Newton decreases $f$ by a fixed amount, then converges quadratically, with bounds free of any constant of $f$.
-   A barrier's parameter $\vartheta$ measures the cost of a central path: $O(\sqrt{\vartheta}\log(1/\varepsilon))$ Newton steps suffice.
-   This is why interior-point methods solve LPs, SOCPs and SDPs in a number of iterations that barely depends on the data.
:::

## 8. Applications: statistics, learning, finance and signal processing {#ch8}

The official syllabus names three fields where convex programs arise. This chapter models a representative problem from each, solves it with the algorithms of ch. 5–7, and reads its dual variables.

### Statistics and machine learning

::: prop
[Proposition 8.1 — Convex maximum likelihood]{.tag} When the density of the observations is log-concave in the parameter, maximum likelihood is a convex program. Logistic regression with labels $y_i \in \{-1, 1\}$ is the main example:
$$
\text{minimize} \ \sum_{i=1}^n \log\big(1 + e^{-y_i x_i^\top \beta}\big) + \frac{\rho}{2}\|\beta\|_2^2 .
$$
Each term is log-sum-exp of $(0, -y_i x_i^\top \beta)$, convex by Propositions 2.4–2.5.

The Hessian is $X^\top D X + \rho I$, where $D$ is diagonal with entries $\sigma(u)(1 - \sigma(u)) \le 1/4$ and $\sigma$ is the logistic function. So the objective is $\rho$-strongly convex and $L$-smooth with
$$
L = \frac14 \|X\|_2^2 + \rho .
$$
:::

::: ex
[Example 8.2 — The LASSO]{.tag} The LASSO (Tibshirani 1996) is the convex program
$$
\text{minimize} \ F(\beta) = \frac{1}{2n}\|y - X\beta\|_2^2 + \lambda \|\beta\|_1 .
$$
Fermat's rule (Proposition 2.9) gives its optimality condition:
$$
\frac{1}{n} X^\top (y - X\beta) \in \lambda \, \partial \|\beta\|_1 .
$$
Each correlation with the residual equals $\lambda \, \mathrm{sign}(\beta_j)$ on the support and lies in $[-\lambda, \lambda]$ off it. In particular $\beta = 0$ is optimal exactly when $\lambda \ge \lambda_{\max} = \|X^\top y\|_\infty / n$.

The code solves a problem with 100 observations, 300 correlated features and 10 true nonzeros, at $\lambda = 0.05 \lambda_{\max}$. The gap $F - F^*$ is:

| iterations | 10 | 100 | 1000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| ISTA | 2.4 | 0.59 | $8.7 \times 10^{-3}$ |
| FISTA | 1.7 | $4.1 \times 10^{-3}$ | $2.6 \times 10^{-7}$ |

The solution has 23 nonzeros, including the 10 true ones, and matches scikit-learn's coordinate descent to $6 \times 10^{-12}$.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n, p, s = 100, 300, 10
C = 0.9 ** np.abs(np.subtract.outer(np.arange(p), np.arange(p)))   # correlated features
X = rng.normal(size=(n, p)) @ np.linalg.cholesky(C).T
beta0 = np.zeros(p); beta0[::30] = rng.choice([-2.0, 2.0], size=s)
y = X @ beta0 + 0.5 * rng.normal(size=n)

lam_max = np.abs(X.T @ y).max() / n             # beta = 0 is optimal above this value
lam = 0.05 * lam_max
F = lambda b: 0.5 / n * np.sum((y - X @ b) ** 2) + lam * np.abs(b).sum()
L = np.linalg.norm(X, 2) ** 2 / n               # Lipschitz constant of the smooth part
soft = lambda v, a: np.sign(v) * np.maximum(np.abs(v) - a, 0.0)
step = lambda b: soft(b - X.T @ (X @ b - y) / (n * L), lam / L)

def ista(K):
    b = np.zeros(p)
    for _ in range(K):
        b = step(b)
    return b

def fista(K):
    b = z = np.zeros(p); t = 1.0
    for _ in range(K):
        b_new = step(z)
        t_new = (1 + np.sqrt(1 + 4 * t * t)) / 2
        z = b_new + (t - 1) / t_new * (b_new - b)
        b, t = b_new, t_new
    return b

ref = Lasso(alpha=lam, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-14, max_iter=1_000_000).fit(X, y).coef_
Fstar = min(F(ref), F(fista(20000)))
print(f"lambda_max = {lam_max:.3f}, lambda = {lam:.4f}, L = {L:.1f}")
for K in (10, 100, 1000):
    print(f"K={K:5d}  ISTA gap {F(ista(K)) - Fstar:.1e}   FISTA gap {F(fista(K)) - Fstar:.1e}")
b = fista(20000)
print("nonzeros:", np.sum(np.abs(b) > 1e-6), " true support recovered:",
      set(np.flatnonzero(beta0)) <= set(np.flatnonzero(np.abs(b) > 1e-6)))
print("max |FISTA - sklearn| =", f"{np.abs(b - ref).max():.1e}")
```

::: note
[Two more convex programs from statistics]{.tag} The support vector machine is a QP whose dual is derived in Ex. 8.

Sparse inverse covariance estimation (Banerjee, El Ghaoui and d'Aspremont 2008; Friedman, Hastie and Tibshirani 2008) maximizes a penalized Gaussian likelihood over $\Theta \succ 0$, given the sample covariance $S$:
$$
\log\det\Theta - \mathrm{tr}(S\Theta) - \rho \sum_{ij} |\Theta_{ij}| .
$$
The nonzero entries of $\Theta$ are the edges of a Gaussian graphical model.
:::

### Finance

::: ex
[Example 8.3 — Markowitz portfolio optimization]{.tag} Asset returns $r \in \mathbb{R}^n$ have mean $\bar r$ and covariance $\Sigma$.

A portfolio $w$ of wealth fractions, $\mathbf{1}^\top w = 1$, has mean return $\bar r^\top w$ and variance $w^\top \Sigma w$. Markowitz (1952) minimizes the risk at a target return:
$$
\text{minimize } w^\top \Sigma w \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \bar r^\top w \ge r_{\min}, \ \ \mathbf{1}^\top w = 1, \ \ w \succeq 0 ,
$$
a QP in which $w \succeq 0$ forbids short sales. Sweeping $r_{\min}$ traces the **efficient frontier**. By Proposition 4.7, the multiplier of the return constraint is the marginal variance of one more unit of return; without $w \succeq 0$ the KKT conditions give the frontier in closed form (Ex. 12).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 8.4 — Value-at-risk and robust constraints are second-order cone constraints]{.tag} If $r \sim \mathcal{N}(\bar r, \Sigma)$ and $\eta \le 1/2$, the constraint $\mathbb{P}(r^\top w \le \alpha) \le \eta$ is equivalent to
$$
\bar r^\top w + \Phi^{-1}(\eta) \, \|\Sigma^{1/2} w\|_2 \ge \alpha ,
$$
an SOC constraint since $\Phi^{-1}(\eta) \le 0$. A linear constraint that must hold for every vector of an ellipsoid is also an SOC constraint (Example 3.5).

::: proof
$r^\top w$ is Gaussian with mean $\bar r^\top w$ and standard deviation $\sigma = \|\Sigma^{1/2} w\|_2$. The probability equals $\Phi((\alpha - \bar r^\top w)/\sigma)$, which is at most $\eta$ exactly when $(\alpha - \bar r^\top w)/\sigma \le \Phi^{-1}(\eta)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### Signal processing

::: ex
[Example 8.5 — Denoising: quadratic smoothing and total variation]{.tag} We observe $y = x + \text{noise}$ with $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and $D$ is the first-difference matrix. Two denoisers compete:
$$
\min_x \ \|x - y\|_2^2 + \rho \|Dx\|_2^2 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \min_x \ \|x - y\|_2^2 + \rho \|Dx\|_1 .
$$
Quadratic smoothing, on the left, is one linear system but blurs jumps. **Total variation**, on the right (Rudin, Osher and Fatemi 1992), keeps jumps: the $\ell_1$ norm tolerates a few large differences.

Writing $\rho \|Dx\|_1 = \max_{\|u\|_\infty \le \rho} u^\top D x$ and minimizing over $x$ gives the dual, a box-constrained QP solved by projected gradient:
$$
\text{minimize} \ \|y - D^\top z\|_2^2 \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \|z\|_\infty \le \rho / 2 ,
$$
